title: How do you read a profit and loss statement in a case interview?
description: A simple walk through a profit and loss statement (income statement): revenue, gross margin, operating costs, EBITDA and net profit, and how they appear in…
hook: You read a profit and loss statement (P&L) from top to bottom, as a story: money comes in as revenue, costs come out in layers, and what is left at each layer is a different measure of profit. In a case, the fastest way to read one is to turn every line into a percentage of revenue and compare years side by side, because the line that grew faster than revenue is usually where the answer is.
body:
From top to bottom

  1. Revenue (also called sales or turnover): all the money earned from customers.
  2. Cost of goods sold (COGS): the direct cost of making or buying what was sold, such as materials and factory labour.
  3. Gross profit = revenue − COGS. Divided by revenue, it gives the gross margin.
  4. Operating costs: the costs of running the business, such as sales and marketing, head office, rent and IT.
  5. EBITDA: earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation. A rough measure of operating cash profit, widely used to value companies.
  6. Depreciation and amortisation: spreading the cost of long-lasting assets, like machines or software, over their useful life.
  7. Operating profit (EBIT), then interest and tax, leaving net profit.

A worked example: one P&L all the way down

An illustrative manufacturer has $100M of revenue, $60M of COGS, $20M of operating costs (excluding depreciation) and $5M of depreciation and amortisation.

  • Gross profit: $100M − $60M = $40M, a 40% gross margin.
  • EBITDA: $40M − $20M = $20M, a 20% margin.
  • EBIT: $20M − $5M = $15M.
  • After $3M of interest, profit before tax is $12M. After $3M of tax (25%), net profit is $9M.

Why does depreciation sit apart? If the company buys a $30M machine that lasts ten years, it does not put $30M through the P&L on day one. It records the machine as an asset and charges about $30M ÷ 10 = $3M a year of depreciation. The cash leaves in year one; the cost reaches profit over ten years. That is why profit and cash are different, and why EBITDA is often used to compare operating performance before those accounting choices.

A worked example: finding the story

A client's revenue grew 10% but operating profit fell by a third. Put each line as a share of revenue:

LineLast year% of revenueThis year% of revenue
Revenue$100M100%$110M100%
COGS$60M60%$66M60%
Gross profit$40M40%$44M40%
Marketing$8M8%$16M14.5%
Other operating costs$20M20%$20M18.2%
Operating profit$12M12%$8M7.3%

Gross margin held at 40%, so gross profit rose $4M. Other costs were flat. Marketing doubled, from $8M to $16M, and that extra $8M more than wiped out the $4M gain. The profit fall is entirely marketing. The next question writes itself: did that spending bring in customers who will pay off later, or was it wasted?

How to read one quickly in a case

  • Convert to percentages of revenue. Changes in percentages show what is really moving.
  • Compare years side by side, and with competitors if you have them.
  • Find the line that grew faster than revenue. That is usually where the story is.
  • Then split that line into price, volume, mix or cost inflation to explain why.

What it sounds like

Weak: "Revenue is up and profit is down, so costs went up. Let me look at each one."
Strong: "Let me put each line as a share of revenue. Gross margin is flat at 40%, so the problem is below gross profit, and marketing has jumped from 8% to about 14.5% of sales. That explains the whole fall."

Common mistakes

  • Comparing absolute numbers only. A cost that grew $2M might be shrinking as a share of a faster-growing business.
  • Treating EBITDA as cash. Capital spending, changes in working capital, interest and tax all use cash that EBITDA ignores.
  • Mixing up profit levels. Gross profit, EBITDA, EBIT and net profit answer different questions. Ask which one the client wants to improve.
  • Confusing margin with markup. See margin versus markup.

Practise

1. Revenue is $80M, COGS $48M, operating costs excluding depreciation $16M and depreciation $4M. What are the gross margin, EBITDA margin and EBIT?

Show the answer

Gross profit $32M, a 40% gross margin. EBITDA $32M − $16M = $16M, a 20% margin. EBIT $16M − $4M = $12M.

2. Revenue rose from $50M to $55M. COGS went from $30M to $35.75M and operating costs from $12M to $12.5M. Why did operating profit fall?

Show the answer

Operating profit fell from $8M to $6.75M. Gross margin dropped from 40% ($20M ÷ $50M) to 35% ($19.25M ÷ $55M), so the problem is the cost of goods or pricing, not overheads. Next, ask whether input costs rose, prices were cut or mix shifted to cheaper products.

3. A company has EBITDA of $20M. It spends $12M on new equipment, its working capital grows by $3M, and it pays $3M of interest and $3M of tax. How much cash did it generate?

Show the answer

$20M − $12M − $3M − $3M − $3M = −$1M. A healthy-looking EBITDA can still mean the company is using cash.

Where to practise next

Read operating leverage to understand why some cost lines swing profit more than others, and how to read a dense table for exhibit practice. The Coastal Brew case, where revenue grew but profit fell, is a good P&L diagnosis to try next.
